title: Adaptive steady-state latency simulator and differential cohort sampler
author: Maya Patel
description: Motivation: production latency tails are often driven by small transient cohorts and phased transitions; existing synthetic runners in benchmark-lab exercise steady throughput but do not faithfully reproduce cohort-driven tail amplification. This PR introduces a lightweight steady-state latency simulator plus a differential cohort sampler that can inject small cohorts with configurable lifecycle, weight, and state-transition patterns. Design highlights: 1) a steady-state detector that learns sequence length distribution and warmup plateau to avoid cold-start bias; 2) cohort sampler that supports temporal cohorts (start, lifetime, fade) and differential noise/priority profiles; 3) a compact stats pipeline that emits per-cohort p50/p95/p99 p99.9 and a small pre-aggregated bucketed histogram suitable for storage in S3; 4) deterministic seeding mode for reproducible regression runs; 5) compatibility layer so the simulator can run as a normal benchlab workload or as a microprobe from perf-canary. Checklist: [x] simulator implementation, [x] sampler logic, [x] exporter and summary CSV, [x] unit + integration tests, [x] docs and quickstart. How to run: python -m benchlab.simulators.steady_state_sim --config=benchlab/configs/cohort_smoke.yaml --seed=42; CI runs a reduced smoke and a full local sample run was executed on a ci-small-gpu pool. Results summary: using the default cohort profile we observed a reproducible p99.9 delta of +14ms when injecting a 3% high-latency cohort (baseline p99.9 210ms -> 224ms) and the sampler scales to 10k req/s with <3% overhead. This PR is intended to provide a more realistic steady-state baseline for subsequent scheduler and KV-cache mitigations and to enable targeted tail-suppression experiments.
